rv.q: Driven by authenticity, earnestness, youth and ample heart, “The Outsiders” is very much an outsider itself.
Perhaps that’s why The Outsiders slides more easily than might be expected into musical form.
For anyone looking for a nostalgic wallow in teen anguish, “The Outsiders” will hit the bull’s-eye.
A musical where the sonic storytelling constantly pales next to the visual one has a bit of a problem on its hands.
But, scenic designers AMP and Tatiana Kahvegian’s tactile set of crunching dirt, exposed scaffolding and tire towers captures more authentic grit than any of the pugnacious characters do.
It packs plenty of heart and soul, but lacks a strong pulse.
But the production only intermittently rises to the challenge of transforming such familiar material into theater that feels both original and necessary.
And yet the musical version of “The Outsiders” that opened on Thursday has been made with so much love and sincerity it survives with most of its heart intact.
The production is the platonic ideal of a retro classic reboot

The show loses its narrative thread in a second act where the requisite narrative tension dissipates instead of intensifying and the show, which lacks the humor of the structurally similar "Newsies," gets stuck in an overly introspective and melancholic loop.
The Outsiders is theatrical gold, and Ponyboy, you are gonna wanna stay with it.
This show is worth coming into a theater!
The Outsiders vibrates with the sort of purposeful storytelling through song that other Broadway newcomers like The Notebook so sorely lack.

The Outsiders succeeds brilliantly at making you feel like you're part of this world, with performances that crackle with authenticity and a production design that puts you right in the middle of 1960s Tulsa.
The Outsiders is energetic, moving, grim, empathetic, and perfectly staged.
The Outsiders is an emotionally and viscerally satisfying work.
By no means the worst musical of the season, The Outsiders still left me disappointed by its lack of a coherent vision.

The story is told with a score by the Texas-born duo Jamestown Revival and Justin Levine, which has a sometimes lilting sometimes hard-charging Southwestern country sound infused with heartfelt harmonies.
...adaptation may have its squabbles, its heart of gold still remains firmly intact.
adaptation of the classic novel rumbles with talent
Perhaps the musical, which will certainly have its share of detractors, might produce a similar effect, and inspire a generation of new theatregoers.
By act two, the show felt like a mechanical procession of plot progression and teen melodrama.
The folk-rock sounding score features some terrific songs, including the two aforementioned numbers and the powerful “Stay Gold,” even if by the end of the evening they all start to sound the same.
It’s a show that feels too desperate to be liked and cried over to truly represent Hinton’s Outsiders.
stunningly violent images that attest to a lot of artistic skill but not much depth

When Ponyboy expresses in song what he’ll bring to being a future writer (“And in his memory, I’ll stay gold”) it also speaks for the creative team and performers, as this production is pure theatrical gold.
When I saw the show, it gripped me from the beginning and held on to me until the end.
The cast and crew are able to make something special that is greater than the sum of its parts.

cn.t: Critics offer mixed-to-positive reviews for this faithful adaptation of S.E. Hinton's novel, praising Danya Taymor's visceral direction and thrilling choreography, particularly a stunning rain-soaked rumble scene, though some find the familiar story forgettable.

lo.t: Lottery opens 12 AM day before performance, closes 3 PM day before. Winners drawn at 10:00 AM and 3:00 PM.
lo.inst: Winners notified by email and have five hours to claim and purchase tickets online. Limit 2.

ru.loc: Bernard B. Jacobs Theatre box office
ru.inst: Available on the day of the performance. Cash or credit card. Limit 2.

so.inst: Available at the box office on the day of the performance only if the show is sold out. Standing positions at the back of the orchestra. Limit 2.

sg.ra: Wikipedia confirms the Jacobs orchestra floor is raked and the house has a single balcony (not two), so Center Orchestra rows A-D get close detail without the second-balcony crush. Playbill's Outsiders guide names Orchestra C Row B Seat 112 the best seat in the house; SeatPlan and Headout both call rows A-D the premium pick for plays specifically. Row numbering 101-114 (center block) means 107/108 sit dead-center on the aisle.

Multiple guides single out Center Orchestra rows F-K as the Jacobs value play: same centered sightline as the A-D premium block, but priced well below because Row I is where the mezzanine overhang line starts (overhead, not yet cutting into the stage). The Jacobs' single-balcony design and raked orchestra floor keep these rows clear, and Wikipedia notes two columns at the rear-of-orchestra promenade supporting the balcony - those sit behind Row N/O, so F-N stay clear of the columns.

SeatPlan and Headout both say the mezzanine overhang 'cuts into the top of the stage' starting at Row O - this is the Jacobs' specific geometry (mezz front at Row I, stage-top cutoff at Row O). Wikipedia adds that the rear-orchestra promenade has two columns supporting the balcony, so patrons here also share space with structural posts. Wheelchair spaces are assigned to rows I, J, P, and R per Headout, confirming P/R are flat promenade rows.

sg.vl: Fine if you pick single-digit seats
sg.ra: Side orchestra uses odd 1-27 (Left) and even 2-28 (Right). SeatPlan notes sightline restrictions intensify at double-digit seats (far aisle) and in back rows. Playbill's Outsiders guide specifically flagged that the right-side front rows were 'a clearer view' than left, because the show's tire set piece on house-left obstructs Orchestra L front rows - this is show-dependent but illustrates the Jacobs' shallow thrust style where side props block near side-orch seats. An AVFMS Orchestra G17 reviewer wrote 'sometimes the boxes block your view of the jungle gym' - the side boxes eat into side-orch sightlines.

sg.vl: Sharp angle, sells as obstructed for a reason
sg.ra: The Jacobs has 2 box seats on each side (16 total per Wikipedia) elevated beside the orchestra. TripAdvisor's theatre rep confirmed obstructed-view seats cluster 'on the extreme sides of the front mezzanine and orchestra' - the boxes are the prime example. Multiple guides warn boxes 'cut off high center stage scenes' and block views of stage-left from the right box / stage-right from the left box. SeatPlan explicitly recommends left boxes over right because the right box loses more stage-left content.

sg.vl: Elevated wide view, 9 rows from stage
sg.ra: SeatPlan names Center Mezz rows A-B the best mezz view in the Jacobs; an AVFMS reviewer at Mezz A107 wrote 'you are perfectly centered and at only nine rows from the stage' - the Jacobs' single-balcony design (per Wikipedia, no second balcony) means the mezz sits close rather than stacked high. Row B dodges Row A's safety-bar issue that SeatPlan calls 'obstructive to shorter patrons.' Front mezz is 168 seats in rows A-D with premium centered sightlines on the full set.

sg.vl: Row E is the legroom hack
sg.ra: Rear mezz is 252 seats in rows E-K. The Jacobs-specific quirk: Row E sits directly behind the front-mezz cross-aisle with a curtain/bannister (not a wall), giving 'extra space' for taller patrons per SeatPlan - Playbill's Outsiders guide confirms Mezz Left Row E has 'a curtained divider between the aisle and row' for extra legroom. Rows G-K are flagged as value seats because the mezz has a 'good rake' and Wikipedia confirms the Jacobs has only one balcony so even Row K stays surprisingly close. An AVFMS Mezz H22 reviewer noted 'legroom is not great' - stick to Row E or aisle seats.

vr.q: Yo, I think we have a new contender for best musical... when I tell you the outsiders was so good.
